modules.title: Probabilistic theories
modules.doc:
A probabilistic theory is described by its ordered real observables and a certain outcome.

## i. Overview

The observables of a physical system form an ordered real vector space. Positive observables are
those whose measured values are never negative. The certain outcome `1` bounds every observable
up to a multiple and sets the scale for measurement outcomes. The order is Archimedean, so no
observable is infinitesimally positive and the certain outcome defines a genuine norm.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory` : ordered real observables with a certain outcome and an Archimedean
  order.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.real` : real-valued outcomes with unit 1.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Observable space and certain outcome
- B. The real numbers

## iv. References

sections.text: ## A. Observable space and certain outcome

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory
declarations.doc: An ordered real observable space with a certain outcome and no infinitesimal observables.
declarations.statement:
structure ProbabilisticTheory where
  /-- The real observables. -/
  Observables : Type*
  /-- Observables can be added and subtracted. -/
  [addCommGroup : AddCommGroup Observables]
  /-- The order saying which observables are positive. -/
  [partialOrder : PartialOrder Observables]
  /-- Observables can be scaled by real numbers. -/
  [module : Module ℝ Observables]
  /-- Adding an observable preserves the order. -/
  [isOrderedAddMonoid : IsOrderedAddMonoid Observables]
  /-- Scaling by a nonnegative real preserves the order. -/
  [posSMulMono : PosSMulMono ℝ Observables]
  /-- The certain outcome. -/
  [one : One Observables]
  /-- The certain outcome is nonnegative. -/
  one_nonneg' : 0 ≤ (1 : Observables)
  /-- Every observable is bounded above by a natural multiple of the certain outcome. -/
  exists_nsmul_one_le' : ∀ B : Observables, ∃ n : ℕ, B ≤ n • (1 : Observables)
  /-- An observable below every positive multiple of the certain outcome is nonpositive. -/
  le_zero_of_forall_pos_smul_one_le' : ∀ A : Observables,
    (∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → A ≤ ε • (1 : Observables)) → A ≤ 0

modules.title: Channels between observable spaces
modules.doc:
Channels preserve positivity and the certain outcome between observable spaces.

## i. Overview

In the order-unit-space model used here, a channel is a positive unital transformation: it sends
observables to observables without turning a possible outcome negative, and it leaves the certain
outcome certain. This covers time evolution, noise, and measurements whose outcomes are discarded
using only ordered real observables and a certain outcome. For quantum systems with a specified
composite structure, physical channels normally require the stronger condition of complete
positivity, which is not expressible using the order-unit structure alone.

A channel `Φ : Channel P Q` is a unital positive linear map from
`P.Observables` to `Q.Observables`.

## ii. Key results

- `Channel` : channels between observable spaces.
- `Channel.id`, `Channel.comp` : the identity and composition of channels.
- `Channel.ofLinearMap` : bundle a linear map after checking positivity and unitality.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Channels between observable spaces

## iv. References

modules.title: Convex spaces of channels
modules.doc:
Random choice between channels and convexity of the resulting space of linear maps.

## i. Overview

A random choice between two channels is again a channel: their convex combination preserves
positivity and the certain outcome. Channels therefore form a convex set inside the real
linear maps between their observable spaces. States inherit this construction as channels
into ℝ.

## ii. Key results

- `Channel.mix` : choose between two channels with a specified probability.
- `Channel.channelSpace_convex` : channels form a convex set of linear maps.
- `Channel.mem_openSegment_iff_exists_mix` : genuine mixtures describe open segments.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Mixing channels
- B. The convex channel space

## iv. References

modules.title: Covariant channels
modules.doc:
Channels that commute with two group actions by reversible transformations.

## i. Overview

More general channels may lose information but can still respect the symmetries of a system. This
is captured by covariance: a channel `Φ` between two spaces carrying group actions `ρ` and `σ` by
reversible transformations is covariant, or intertwining, if

`Φ ∘ ρ g = σ g ∘ Φ` for every group element `g`.

A reversible transformation is covariant
exactly when the target action is the transport of the source action. Together with the reversible
transformations, this gives a common framework for symmetries and dynamics of observable spaces.

## ii. Key results

- `Channel.IsIntertwining`: Covariance of a channel under two group actions.
- `Channel.isIntertwining_iff_eq_transport`: Characterization of the transported action.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Covariant channels
  - A.1. Definition and closure properties
- B. Covariance of transport

## iv. References

modules.title: Channels are contractions
modules.doc:
Unital positive linear maps are contractions with respect to the order-unit norm and are
therefore continuous.

## i. Overview

An observable lies between the positive and negative multiples of the certain outcome set by
its order-unit norm. A channel preserves both inequalities and the certain outcome, so the
same bound holds for its image.

## ii. Key results

- `Channel.norm_apply_le`: Channels are contractions.
- `Channel.continuous`: Channels are continuous.
- `Channel.toContinuousLinearMap`: Channels as continuous linear maps.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Contractivity and continuity

## iv. References

modules.title: Reversible transformations of observables
modules.doc:
Reversible transformations of observables, their group structure and transport of group actions.

## i. Overview

Time evolution, spatial symmetries and changes of reference frame all have something in common:
they transform observables in a way that can be undone.

This motivates reversible transformations, defined as unital linear order isomorphisms of
observable spaces. They form a group. A group representation by
reversible transformations describes symmetries or reversible dynamics. For example, time evolution
is represented by the additive group of real numbers. A reversible transformation also transports a
group action from one observable space to another by conjugation.

## ii. Key results

- `Reversible`: Reversible transformations, i.e. unital linear order isomorphisms of
  observable spaces.
- `Reversible.toChannelHom`: Reversible transformations embed in the monoid of channels.
- `Reversible.transport`: Transport of a group action along a reversible transformation.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Reversible transformations
  - A.1. Definition
  - A.2. Group structure
  - A.3. As channels
- B. Transport of group actions
  - B.1. Conjugation
  - B.2. Transported actions

## iv. References

modules.title: Classical probabilistic theories
modules.doc:
In a classical system every observable has a definite value in each configuration.

## i. Overview

An observable of a classical system with configurations `X` is a bounded real function on `X`.
A closed algebra `S` of bounded functions fixes which functions count as observables. On a
measurable space these are the bounded measurable functions.

The observables in `S` form the probabilistic theory `classical S`. Observables add, multiply and
compare value by value. Their algebra is commutative, which is characteristic of classical
systems.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.classical` : the classical theory of a closed algebra of bounded functions.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.Classical.instFunLike` : the value of an observable in a configuration.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.Classical.le_def` : observables are ordered by their values.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The classical theory
- B. Values of observables

## iv. References

modules.title: Dirac states
modules.doc:
A classical system in a definite configuration is in a pure state.

## i. Overview

The Dirac state at a configuration `x` assigns to each observable its value at `x`. It describes
a classical system whose configuration is known exactly, so every observable has vanishing
variance. Conversely, a state in which every observable has vanishing variance around its value
at `x` is the Dirac state at `x`. Dirac states are therefore pure.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.Classical.dirac` : the Dirac state at a configuration.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.Classical.eq_dirac_iff` : the Dirac state is the state in which every
  observable has a sharp value.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.Classical.isPure_dirac` : Dirac states are pure.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Dirac states
- B. Sharp values
- C. Purity

## iv. References

modules.title: The observables of a C⋆-algebra
modules.doc:
The self-adjoint part of a unital C⋆-algebra is an Archimedean order-unit space.

## i. Overview

The observables of a quantum system are the self-adjoint elements of its C⋆-algebra. One
observable lies below another if their difference has no negative measurement outcome. The
identity is the certain outcome.

Every observable lies below a multiple of the identity. So no outcome exceeds the norm.

An observable that lies below every positive multiple of the identity has no positive outcome.
This is the Archimedean property.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.selfAdjoint_le_nsmul_one_ceil_norm` : bound observables by natural
  multiples of the identity.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.selfAdjoint_le_zero_of_forall_pos_smul_one_le` : an observable below
  every positive multiple of the identity is nonpositive.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.ofCStarAlgebra` : the self-adjoint observables of a quantum system.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.realEquivComplex` : real outcomes are the self-adjoint complex scalars.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The order-unit space of observables
- B. The Archimedean property
- C. Quantum observables and scalar outcomes

## iv. References

modules.title: Channels of C⋆-algebras
modules.doc:
Channels between the self-adjoint parts of C⋆-algebras extend uniquely to all operators.

## i. Overview

A channel acts on self-adjoint observables. Every operator decomposes into self-adjoint
real and imaginary parts, so a channel extends uniquely to a complex-linear map on all
operators. This extension is positive and preserves the identity. Restricting a unital positive
complex-linear map to observables recovers a channel.

## ii. Key results

- `Channel.complexExtension` : extend a real-linear map on self-adjoint elements.
- `Channel.complexExtension_unique` : uniqueness of the complex-linear extension.
- `Channel.extend` : a channel extended to all operators.
- `Channel.ofComplex` : a unital positive map restricted to a channel.
- `Channel.complexEquiv` : channels are the same as unital positive maps between all operators.
- `Channel.extend_comp` : extension respects composition.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Complex extension
  - A.1. The extension
  - A.2. Agreement and uniqueness
- B. Channels on all operators

## iv. References

declarations.doc:

modules.title: States of a C⋆-algebra
modules.doc:
States inherit complex extension from channels and can be characterized by traciality.

## i. Overview

A state assigns real expectation values to self-adjoint operators, the observables.
Every operator has a decomposition into self-adjoint parts, its real and imaginary part.
Applying states onto these two parts is a unique extension to a complex-linear map and vice versa.
Therefore complex-linear maps are in bijection with their restriction to self-adjoint operators.

A state is a channel into ℝ. The scalar identification
`realEquivComplex` lets it inherit complex extension from the channel construction.
A tracial state assigns the same expectation to the positive observables `a⋆a` and `aa⋆`.
Equivalently its complex extension is cyclic on products.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.extend` : complex expectation values on all operators.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.complexEquiv` : states correspond to normalized positive
  complex-linear functionals.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.extend_comap` : extension respects state pullback.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.IsTracial` : equality of expectations on `a⋆a` and `aa⋆`.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.isTracial_iff_extend_map_mul_comm` : traciality is equivalent to
  cyclicity of the complex extension.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. States on all operators
- B. Tracial states

## iv. References

modules.title: Tracial functionals
modules.doc:
A functional on an algebra is tracial if the order of a product does not change its value.

## i. Overview

A functional `f` on an algebra is tracial if `f (x y) = f (y x)` for all `x` and `y`. The order
of a product does not change its value.

On an algebra with an adjoint it is enough to check `f (x⋆ x) = f (x x⋆)`. An operator and its
adjoint then give the same value in both orders.

## ii. Key results

- `LinearMap.map_mul_comm_iff_star_mul_self_eq_mul_star_self` : `f` is tracial if and only if
  `f (x⋆ * x) = f (x * x⋆)` for all `x`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Checking cyclicity on `x⋆ x`

## iv. References

modules.title: Effects
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

An effect models a yes/no measurement outcome, ranging continuously between the impossible
outcome `0` and the certain outcome `1`. Formally, it is a point of the order interval `[0, 1]`
inside `P.Observables`. For self-adjoint matrices, effects are exactly the operators
`0 ≤ M ≤ 1` — the elements of a POVM.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.Effect` : a bounded measurement outcome, the
  order interval `[0, 1]` of its observables.
- `Effect.mem_iff_mem_posCone_and_one_sub_mem_posCone` : an effect is exactly a positive element
  whose complement from the order unit is also positive.
- `Effect.exists_pos_smul_mem` : every positive observable becomes an effect after scaling it down
  enough.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Effects

## iv. References

- G. Ludwig, *Foundations of Quantum Mechanics I*, Springer, 1983.
  <https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-86751-4>

declarations.statement:
lemma mem_iff_mem_posCone_and_one_sub_mem_posCone {A : P.Observables} :
    A ∈ P.Effect ↔ A ∈ PosCone P ∧ 1 - A ∈ PosCone P

modules.title: Complementary effects
modules.doc:
The complement `1 - e` of an effect, its antitonicity and compatibility with mixtures.

## i. Overview

The complement of an effect `e` is the yes/no test that fires exactly when `e` doesn't: `1 - e`.
Physically, a state's probability of "no" is always `1` minus its probability of "yes".

## ii. Key results

- `Effect.complement` : the complementary effect `1 - e`.
- `Effect.complement_antitone` : the complement reverses order.
- `Effect.complement_mix` : the complement of a mixture is the mixture of the complements.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The complement
- B. Monotonicity of the complement
- C. The complement and mixtures

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: Convexity and mixtures of effects
modules.doc:
The effect interval is convex, so effects can be mixed with a given probability.

## i. Overview

The effect interval `[0, 1]` is convex: randomizing between two effects with some probability
gives back an effect. Physically, flipping a biased coin to decide which of two measurements to
actually run is itself a legitimate measurement.

## ii. Key results

- `Effect.convex` : the effect interval is convex.
- `Effect.mix` : randomize between two effects with a given probability.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Convexity and mixtures of effects

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: The metric space of effects
modules.doc:
The order-unit metric on effects and their identification with the order-unit-norm ball.

## i. Overview

Effects sit inside `P.Observables`. Pulling back the order-unit norm along this inclusion
gives them a metric space structure for free.

Effects also correspond to points of the order-unit-norm ball, by the affine rescaling
`e ↦ 2 • e - 1` that turns `[0, 1]` into the symmetric `[-1, 1]` the norm itself ranges over.

## ii. Key results

- `Effect.dist_eq_orderUnitNorm` : the effect metric is the order-unit norm of the difference.
- `Effect.effectEquiv` : effects correspond to points of the order-unit-norm ball.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The effect metric
- B. Effects as points of the order-unit-norm ball

## iv. References

* None.

modules.title: Sharp effects
modules.doc:
Sharp effects: extreme points of the effect interval, preserved by taking complements.

## i. Overview

The effect interval `[0, 1]` is convex. A sharp effect is an extreme point of it: one that cannot
be written as a nontrivial mixture of two distinct effects. Sharp effects generalize projections.

## ii. Key results

- `Effect.IsSharp` : an effect that cannot be written as a nontrivial mixture of two distinct
  effects.
- `Effect.isSharp_complement_iff` : sharpness is preserved by taking the complement.

## iii. Table of contents

modules.title: Local nets of observables
modules.doc:
Observables of subsystems and their inclusion into larger subsystems.

## i. Overview

Let `R` index subsystems, with `X ≤ Y` meaning that `X` is contained in `Y`. The observables of
`X` are given by `(A X).Observables`. A local net assigns to `X ≤ Y` a channel,
which regards an observable of `X` as one of `Y`.

For a tensor product system with `H_Y ≃ H_X ⊗ H_rest`, `(A X).Observables` consists of Hermitian
operators on `H_X`. Inclusion acts by `M ↦ M ⊗ 1`: this acts as `M` on `X` and
as the identity on the remaining factors.

The local observables can also be viewed in one space, `N.Quasilocal`, the algebraic direct limit
of the local observable spaces. It is a real vector space and carries no norm. Completing it in a
norm, which needs more structure than is assumed here, gives the quasilocal algebra of the physics
literature. Inductive limits of order-unit spaces are developed in [ref: arxiv_1705_04663].

## ii. Key results

- `LocalNet`: subsystem observables with channels into larger subsystems.
- `LocalNet.IsOrderEmbedding`: the inclusion maps reflect order.
- `LocalNet.map_le_map_iff`: inclusion preserves and reflects inequalities.
- `LocalNet.incl_injective`: order-embedding inclusion maps are injective.
- `LocalNet.Quasilocal`: the algebraic direct limit of the local observable spaces.
- `LocalNet.toQuasilocal`: regard an observable of one subsystem as a quasilocal observable.
- `LocalNet.toQuasilocal_eq_iff`: equality of quasilocal observables can be checked in a common
  larger subsystem.
- `LocalNet.toQuasilocal_injective`: order-embedding inclusions keep local observables distinct.
- `LocalNet.exists_toQuasilocal_eq`, `exists_toQuasilocal_eq₂`: quasilocal observables have
  representatives in a single subsystem, and any two have representatives in a common one.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Subsystems and inclusions
- B. Order-embedding inclusions
- C. The quasilocal observable space
- D. Embedding the local observables
- E. Directed families of subsystems

## iv. References

* L. Mawhinney, I. G. Todorov, *Inductive limits in the operator system and related categories*,
  arXiv:1705.04663. [ref: arxiv_1705_04663]

sections.text:
## C. The quasilocal observable space

For a directed family of subsystems, observables from different subsystems can be included in a
common larger one and combined there. The direct limit identifies all such local descriptions
consistently and supplies the resulting real vector space.

## D. Embedding the local observables

The map `toQuasilocal N i` takes an observable of subsystem `i` to the quasilocal observable it
represents.

## E. Directed families of subsystems

If any two subsystems are contained in a common larger one, the quasilocal observable space is
described by representatives in single subsystems.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet
declarations.doc: The observables of each subsystem, with channels into larger subsystems.
declarations.statement:
structure ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet (R : Type*) [Preorder R] (A : R → ProbabilisticTheory) where
  /-- Regard an observable of `X` as an observable of `Y` when `X ≤ Y`. -/
  incl : ∀ {X Y : R}, X ≤ Y → Channel (A X) (A Y)
  /-- Inclusion into the same subsystem is the identity. -/
  incl_refl : ∀ X : R, incl (le_refl X) = .id (A X)
  /-- Including through an intermediate subsystem agrees with direct inclusion. -/
  incl_trans : ∀ {X Y Z : R} (h₁ : X ≤ Y) (h₂ : Y ≤ Z) (h₃ : X ≤ Z),
    incl h₃ = (incl h₂).comp (incl h₁)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.incl_refl_apply
declarations.doc: An observable is unchanged by inclusion into the same subsystem.
declarations.statement:
lemma incl_refl_apply (N : LocalNet R A) (X : R) (a : (A X).Observables) :
    N.incl (le_refl X) a = a

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.incl_trans_apply
declarations.doc: Including an observable through an intermediate subsystem agrees with direct inclusion.
declarations.statement:
lemma incl_trans_apply (N : LocalNet R A) (h₁ : X ≤ Y) (h₂ : Y ≤ Z) (h₃ : X ≤ Z)
    (a : (A X).Observables) :
    N.incl h₃ a = N.incl h₂ (N.incl h₁ a)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.IsOrderEmbedding
declarations.doc: The inclusion maps are order embeddings if each reflects positivity.
declarations.statement:
class IsOrderEmbedding (N : LocalNet R A) : Prop where
  /-- An observable that is positive in a larger subsystem is already positive in the smaller. -/
  nonneg_of_incl_nonneg : ∀ {X Y : R} (h : X ≤ Y) {a : (A X).Observables}, 0 ≤ N.incl h a → 0 ≤ a

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.map_le_map_iff
declarations.doc: Inclusion in an order-embedding net preserves and reflects inequalities.
declarations.statement:
lemma map_le_map_iff (N : LocalNet R A) [N.IsOrderEmbedding] (h : X ≤ Y) {a b : (A X).Observables} :
    N.incl h a ≤ N.incl h b ↔ a ≤ b

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.incl_injective
declarations.doc: The inclusion maps of an order-embedding net are injective.
declarations.statement:
lemma incl_injective (N : LocalNet R A) [N.IsOrderEmbedding] (h : X ≤ Y) :
    Function.Injective (N.incl h)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.inclLin
declarations.doc:
The inclusions as linear maps: the transition maps of the direct limit defining
`N.Quasilocal`.
declarations.statement:
abbrev inclLin (N : LocalNet R A) (X Y : R) (h : X ≤ Y) :
    (A X).Observables →ₗ[ℝ] (A Y).Observables

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.directedSystem
declarations.doc:
The inclusions form a directed system: including a subsystem into itself does nothing, and
successive inclusions compose.
declarations.statement:
instance directedSystem (N : LocalNet R A) :
    DirectedSystem (fun X => (A X).Observables) fun i j h => N.inclLin i j h

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.Quasilocal
declarations.doc: The algebraic direct limit of the local observable spaces.
declarations.statement: def Quasilocal (N : LocalNet R A) : Type _

declarations.doc: Quasilocal observables add, as elements of a direct limit of vector spaces.
declarations.statement: noncomputable instance : AddCommGroup N.Quasilocal

declarations.doc: Quasilocal observables can be scaled by real numbers.
declarations.statement: noncomputable instance : Module ℝ N.Quasilocal

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal
declarations.doc: Regard an observable of subsystem `i` as a quasilocal observable.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def toQuasilocal (N : LocalNet R A) (i : R) : (A i).Observables →ₗ[ℝ] N.Quasilocal

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal_incl
declarations.doc: Including an observable in a larger subsystem does not change its quasilocal representation.
declarations.statement:
lemma toQuasilocal_incl {i j : R} (h : i ≤ j) (a : (A i).Observables) :
    toQuasilocal N j (N.incl h a) = toQuasilocal N i a

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal_eq_of_incl_eq
declarations.doc:
Observables that agree in a common larger subsystem represent the same quasilocal
observable.
declarations.statement:
lemma toQuasilocal_eq_of_incl_eq {i j k : R} (hik : i ≤ k) (hjk : j ≤ k)
    {a : (A i).Observables} {b : (A j).Observables} (h : N.incl hik a = N.incl hjk b) :
    toQuasilocal N i a = toQuasilocal N j b

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.exists_incl_eq_of_toQuasilocal_eq
declarations.doc:
Observables representing the same quasilocal observable agree in a common larger
subsystem.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal_eq_iff
declarations.doc:
Two local observables represent the same quasilocal observable exactly when they agree in a
common larger subsystem.
declarations.statement:
lemma toQuasilocal_eq_iff {i j : R} (a : (A i).Observables) (b : (A j).Observables) :
    toQuasilocal N i a = toQuasilocal N j b ↔
      ∃ (k : R) (hik : i ≤ k) (hjk : j ≤ k), N.incl hik a = N.incl hjk b

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toQuasilocal_injective
declarations.doc: Order-embedding inclusions keep distinct local observables distinct in the quasilocal space.
declarations.statement:
lemma toQuasilocal_injective [N.IsOrderEmbedding] (i : R) :
    Function.Injective (toQuasilocal N i)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.exists_toQuasilocal_eq
declarations.doc: Every quasilocal observable has a representative in some subsystem.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_toQuasilocal_eq (x : N.Quasilocal) :
    ∃ (i : R) (a : (A i).Observables), toQuasilocal N i a = x

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.exists_toQuasilocal_eq₂
declarations.doc: Any two quasilocal observables have representatives in a common subsystem.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_toQuasilocal_eq₂ (x y : N.Quasilocal) :
    ∃ (i : R) (a b : (A i).Observables), toQuasilocal N i a = x ∧ toQuasilocal N i b = y

modules.title: Interactions on a local net
modules.doc:
An interaction is a family of local observables, each associated with a region of the net.

## i. Overview

Extensive observables such as energy, magnetization and particle number can be expressed as
sums of local terms. An interaction assigns a supporting region and an observable to each
label. Each term can be included into any larger region and is taken to be zero when its
support is not contained in the region.

## ii. Key results

- `Interaction`: A family of local observables with specified supports.
- `Interaction.termIn`: An interaction term expressed in a given region.
- `Interaction.incl_termIn`: Compatibility with inclusions of regions.
- `Interaction.termIn_add`: Compatibility with addition.
- `Interaction.termIn_smul`: Compatibility with scalar multiplication.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Interactions
- B. Interaction terms in a region

## iv. References

sections.text: ## B. Interaction terms in a region

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction
declarations.doc: A family of local observables on `N`, indexed by `ι`, with specified supports.
declarations.statement:
structure ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction {R : Type*} [Preorder R]
    {A : R → ProbabilisticTheory} (N : LocalNet R A) (ι : Type*) where
  /-- The supporting region of each term. -/
  supp : ι → R
  /-- The observable associated with each term. -/
  term : ∀ i, (A (supp i)).Observables

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.labelsIn
declarations.doc: The labels of terms supported in `Λ`.
declarations.statement: def labelsIn (Λ : R) : Set ι

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.termIn
declarations.doc: The term `i` expressed in `Λ`, or zero if its support is not contained in `Λ`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def termIn (Λ : R) (i : ι) : (A Λ).Observables

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.incl_termIn
declarations.doc:
Including a term from `Λ` into `Λ'` agrees with evaluating it in `Λ'` whenever
its support is contained in `Λ`, and gives zero otherwise.
declarations.statement:
lemma incl_termIn {Λ Λ' : R} (h : Λ ≤ Λ') (i : ι) :
    N.incl h (Φ.termIn Λ i) = (Φ.labelsIn Λ).indicator (Φ.termIn Λ') i

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.termIn_add
declarations.doc: Evaluating interaction terms in a region preserves addition.
declarations.statement:
lemma termIn_add (s : ι → R) (t t' : ∀ i, (A (s i)).Observables) (Λ : R) (i : ι) :
    (⟨s, t + t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i =
      (⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i +
        (⟨s, t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.termIn_smul
declarations.doc: Evaluating interaction terms in a region preserves scalar multiplication.
declarations.statement:
lemma termIn_smul (s : ι → R) (c : ℝ) (t : ∀ i, (A (s i)).Observables) (Λ : R) (i : ι) :
    (⟨s, c • t⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i =
      c • (⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ i

modules.title: Integrating interactions over local regions
modules.doc:
An interaction defines a local observable by integrating its terms over a region.

## i. Overview

The integral of an interaction gives an observable in each region. The choice of measure allows
both discrete sums and continuum integrals.

For nested regions, the observable in the larger region decomposes into the observable of the
smaller region and the remaining interaction terms. For two regions with disjoint sets of
supported terms, the observable decomposes into their contributions and the terms supported
in neither region.

## ii. Key results

- `Interaction.sumIn`: The integral of interaction terms in a region.
- `Interaction.norm_sumIn_le`: A norm bound for the integral.
- `Interaction.sumIn_add`, `Interaction.sumIn_smul`: Linearity of integration.
- `Interaction.sumIn_split`: Decomposition for nested regions.
- `Interaction.sumIn_disjoint`: Decomposition for regions with disjoint sets of terms.
- `Interaction.sumIn_count`, `Interaction.sumIn_count_tsum`: Discrete sums over finite or
  countable labels.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Integration over a region
- B. Nested regions
- C. Disjoint regions
- D. Discrete interactions

## iv. References

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.norm_termIn_le
declarations.doc: The norm of a term cannot increase when included into another region.
declarations.statement: lemma norm_termIn_le (Λ : R) (i : ι) : ‖Φ.termIn Λ i‖ ≤ ‖Φ.term i‖

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn
declarations.doc: The observable in `Λ` obtained by integrating the interaction terms supported there.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def sumIn (Λ : R) : (A Λ).Observables

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.norm_sumIn_le
declarations.doc: The norm of the integral is bounded by the integral of the norms.
declarations.statement: lemma norm_sumIn_le (Λ : R) : ‖Φ.sumIn μ Λ‖ ≤ ∫ i, ‖Φ.termIn Λ i‖ ∂μ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_add
declarations.doc: Integration preserves addition of interaction terms with the same supports.
declarations.statement:
lemma sumIn_add (s : ι → R) (t t' : ∀ i, (A (s i)).Observables) {Λ : R}
    (h : Integrable ((⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ) μ)
    (h' : Integrable ((⟨s, t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).termIn Λ) μ) :
    (⟨s, t + t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ =
      (⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ + (⟨s, t'⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_smul
declarations.doc: Integration preserves scalar multiplication of interaction terms.
declarations.statement:
lemma sumIn_smul (s : ι → R) (c : ℝ) (t : ∀ i, (A (s i)).Observables) (Λ : R) :
    (⟨s, c • t⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ =
      c • (⟨s, t⟩ : Interaction N ι).sumIn μ Λ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.setIntegral_labelsIn
declarations.doc:
Integrating the terms supported in `Λ` in a larger region `Λ'` agrees with including
the integral over `Λ` into `Λ'`.
declarations.statement:
lemma setIntegral_labelsIn {Λ Λ' : R} (h : Λ ≤ Λ') (hS : MeasurableSet (Φ.labelsIn Λ))
    (h1 : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ) μ) :
    ∫ i in Φ.labelsIn Λ, Φ.termIn Λ' i ∂μ = N.incl h (Φ.sumIn μ Λ)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.coupling
declarations.doc: The contribution in `Λ'` from terms not supported in `Λ`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def coupling (Λ Λ' : R) : (A Λ').Observables

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_split
declarations.doc:
The observable in a larger region is the included observable of the smaller region
plus the remaining interaction terms.
declarations.statement:
lemma sumIn_split {Λ Λ' : R} (h : Λ ≤ Λ') (hS : MeasurableSet (Φ.labelsIn Λ))
    (h1 : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ) μ) (h2 : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ') μ) :
    Φ.sumIn μ Λ' = N.incl h (Φ.sumIn μ Λ) + Φ.coupling μ Λ Λ'

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.crossingIn
declarations.doc: The contribution in `Λ` from terms supported in neither `Λ₁` nor `Λ₂`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def crossingIn (Λ₁ Λ₂ Λ : R) : (A Λ).Observables

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_disjoint
declarations.doc:
For regions with disjoint sets of supported terms, the observable in a common larger
region is the sum of their included observables and the remaining interaction terms.
declarations.statement:
lemma sumIn_disjoint {Λ₁ Λ₂ Λ : R} (h₁ : Λ₁ ≤ Λ) (h₂ : Λ₂ ≤ Λ)
    (hd : Disjoint (Φ.labelsIn Λ₁) (Φ.labelsIn Λ₂)) (m₁ : MeasurableSet (Φ.labelsIn Λ₁))
    (m₂ : MeasurableSet (Φ.labelsIn Λ₂)) (g₁ : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ₁) μ)
    (g₂ : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ₂) μ) (g : Integrable (Φ.termIn Λ) μ) :
    Φ.sumIn μ Λ = N.incl h₁ (Φ.sumIn μ Λ₁) + N.incl h₂ (Φ.sumIn μ Λ₂) +
      Φ.crossingIn μ Λ₁ Λ₂ Λ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_count
declarations.doc: With finitely many labels, integration against the counting measure is a finite sum.
declarations.statement:
lemma sumIn_count [Fintype ι] (Λ : R) :
    Φ.sumIn Measure.count Λ = ∑ i, Φ.termIn Λ i

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Interaction.sumIn_count_tsum
declarations.doc:
With countably many labels, integration against the counting measure is an infinite sum,
provided the terms are integrable.

modules.title: Order-unit structure on quasilocal observables
modules.doc:
Positivity and a common unit for observables assembled from a local net.

## i. Overview

The quasilocal construction treats observables from different subsystems as observables of one
global system. A quantity measured locally can also be described in a larger subsystem; these
descriptions must refer to the same physical quantity. For the global description to work, it must
preserve more than identity: whether an observable is positive, how it compares with other
observables, and what represents the certain outcome.

This file shows how those properties carry over from the local systems. Positive local observables
give the quasilocal space its notion of positivity, and the local copies of `1` give it one certain
observable. Local observables thereby retain their interpretation as observables of the whole
system. The resulting order-unit structure lets a state of the global system assign positive,
normalized expectations to them.

## ii. Key results

- `LocalNet.positive`: the global observables with a positive local representative.
- `LocalNet.toQuasilocal_nonneg_iff`: local and global positivity agree when inclusions
  reflect order.
- `LocalNet.toQuasilocalChannel`: each subsystem maps to the global observable space
  by a channel.
- `LocalNet.quasilocalTheory`: the global observables with their order and unit, inherited
  from the subsystems.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Positivity
- B. The common order unit
- C. The order
- D. Global observables and local channels

## iv. References

sections.text:
## A. Positivity

An observable assembled from local pieces is positive when it has a positive local description.
Positive observables from different subsystems can be brought into a common larger subsystem and
added there. Nonnegative scaling preserves positivity within any one subsystem.

## B. The common order unit

The certain observable must not depend on which subsystem describes it. Every inclusion preserves
`1`, so the local units all represent one global observable.

## C. The order

A comparison `x ≤ y` means that `y - x` has a positive local description. This is a partial order:
an observable cannot be both positive and negative unless it is zero. When inclusions reflect
order, comparisons made within a subsystem agree with comparisons in the global system.

## D. Global observables and local channels

Every global observable has a local representative bounded by a multiple of the local unit.
These bounds give the global unit its order-unit property. Order-reflecting inclusions also
carry the local Archimedean property to the global space. Each subsystem then maps into the
global observable space by a channel.

modules.title: Archimedean order-unit spaces
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

The Archimedean condition is a regularity assumption on an order-unit space that rules out
infinitesimal elements. With it, the order and the distinguished unit `1` determine a natural
norm,

`‖A‖₁ = inf {r ≥ 0 | -r • 1 ≤ A ≤ r • 1}`.

Thus the unit interval sets the scale for the observables: `[-1, 1]` is exactly the closed unit
ball. For self-adjoint matrices, this recovers the usual operator norm. Concretely, this is the
Minkowski functional of the order interval `[-1, 1]`: convexity of that interval gives the triangle
inequality, and its symmetry gives homogeneity, for free. The Archimedean condition is only needed
afterwards, to upgrade this from a seminorm to a genuine norm.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_eq_zero_iff` : the order-unit norm separates points.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.closedIciTopology` : the positive cone is closed in the order-unit-norm
  topology.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Archimedean order units
- B. The order-unit bounds and norm
- C. Norm axioms
- D. The induced normed space
- E. Order-closedness of the topology

## iv. References

    (h : ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → A ≤ ε • (1 : P.Observables)) : A ≤ 0

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitBounds_bddBelow
declarations.doc: The order-unit bounds are bounded below by `0`.
declarations.statement: lemma orderUnitBounds_bddBelow (A : P.Observables) : BddBelow (orderUnitBounds A)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_le
declarations.doc: Any order-unit bound on `A` is an upper bound for `A`'s order-unit norm.
declarations.statement:
lemma orderUnitNorm_le {A : P.Observables} {r : ℝ} (hr : r ∈ orderUnitBounds A) :
    orderUnitNorm A ≤ r

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitBounds_nonempty
declarations.doc: Every element has some order-unit bound.
declarations.statement: lemma orderUnitBounds_nonempty (A : P.Observables) : (orderUnitBounds A).Nonempty

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_nonneg
declarations.doc: The order-unit norm is an infimum of nonnegative reals, hence itself nonnegative.
declarations.statement: lemma orderUnitNorm_nonneg (A : P.Observables) : 0 ≤ orderUnitNorm A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_zero
declarations.statement: lemma orderUnitNorm_zero : orderUnitNorm (0 : P.Observables) = 0

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitBounds_neg
declarations.doc:
Negation preserves the set of order-unit bounds: a symmetric interval bounding `A` bounds
`-A` too.
declarations.statement: lemma orderUnitBounds_neg (A : P.Observables) : orderUnitBounds (-A) = orderUnitBounds A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_neg
declarations.statement: lemma orderUnitNorm_neg (A : P.Observables) : orderUnitNorm (-A) = orderUnitNorm A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.add_mem_orderUnitBounds
declarations.doc: A bound for `A` and a bound for `B` add up to a bound for `A + B`.
declarations.statement:
lemma add_mem_orderUnitBounds {A B : P.Observables} {r s : ℝ} (hr : r ∈ orderUnitBounds A)
    (hs : s ∈ orderUnitBounds B) : r + s ∈ orderUnitBounds (A + B)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.exists_orderUnitBound_lt
declarations.doc: There is an order-unit bound on `A` within `ε` of its norm.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_orderUnitBound_lt (A : P.Observables) {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ r ∈ orderUnitBounds A, r < orderUnitNorm A + ε

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_add_le
declarations.statement:
lemma orderUnitNorm_add_le (A B : P.Observables) :
    orderUnitNorm (A + B) ≤ orderUnitNorm A + orderUnitNorm B

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.smul_one_mono
declarations.doc:
Scaling the unit by a larger nonnegative real gives a larger multiple: `r ↦ r • 1` is
monotone.
declarations.statement:
lemma smul_one_mono {r s : ℝ} (hrs : r ≤ s) :
    r • (1 : P.Observables) ≤ s • (1 : P.Observables)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.le_orderUnitNorm_smul_one
declarations.doc: Every element is bounded above by its order-unit norm times `1`.
declarations.statement:
lemma le_orderUnitNorm_smul_one (A : P.Observables) :
    A ≤ orderUnitNorm A • (1 : P.Observables)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.neg_orderUnitNorm_smul_one_le
declarations.doc: `A` is also bounded below by `-(orderUnitNorm A • 1)`.
declarations.statement:
lemma neg_orderUnitNorm_smul_one_le (A : P.Observables) :
    -(orderUnitNorm A • (1 : P.Observables)) ≤ A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_mem_orderUnitBounds
declarations.doc:
The norm itself is an order-unit bound, i.e. the infimum defining `orderUnitNorm` is a
minimum.
declarations.statement: lemma orderUnitNorm_mem_orderUnitBounds (A : P.Observables) : orderUnitNorm A ∈ orderUnitBounds A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.le_smul_one_of_orderUnitNorm_lt
declarations.doc: An element with order-unit norm strictly below `ε` is itself bounded above by `ε • 1`.
declarations.statement:
lemma le_smul_one_of_orderUnitNorm_lt {A : P.Observables} {ε : ℝ} (h : orderUnitNorm A < ε) :
    A ≤ ε • (1 : P.Observables)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.neg_smul_one_le_of_orderUnitNorm_lt
declarations.doc: The mirror image of `le_smul_one_of_orderUnitNorm_lt`.
declarations.statement:
lemma neg_smul_one_le_of_orderUnitNorm_lt {A : P.Observables} {ε : ℝ} (h : orderUnitNorm A < ε) :
    -(ε • (1 : P.Observables)) ≤ A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_le_iff
declarations.doc: The order-unit norm is characterized exactly by its symmetric order interval.
declarations.statement:
lemma orderUnitNorm_le_iff {A : P.Observables} {r : ℝ} :
    orderUnitNorm A ≤ r ↔ 0 ≤ r ∧ -(r • (1 : P.Observables)) ≤ A ∧ A ≤ r • (1 : P.Observables)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_eq_zero_iff
declarations.doc: The order-unit norm is definite: `‖A‖₁ = 0` forces `A = 0`.
declarations.statement: lemma orderUnitNorm_eq_zero_iff {A : P.Observables} : orderUnitNorm A = 0 ↔ A = 0

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_smul_le
declarations.doc: Nonnegative scalar multiplication scales the order-unit norm from above.
declarations.statement:
lemma orderUnitNorm_smul_le {r : ℝ} (hr : 0 ≤ r) (A : P.Observables) :
    orderUnitNorm (r • A) ≤ r * orderUnitNorm A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_smul_of_pos
declarations.doc: Positive scalar multiplication scales the order-unit norm.
declarations.statement:
lemma orderUnitNorm_smul_of_pos {r : ℝ} (hr : 0 < r) (A : P.Observables) :
    orderUnitNorm (r • A) = r * orderUnitNorm A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNorm_smul
declarations.doc: The order-unit norm is absolutely homogeneous.
declarations.statement:
lemma orderUnitNorm_smul (r : ℝ) (A : P.Observables) :
    orderUnitNorm (r • A) = |r| * orderUnitNorm A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.exists_orderUnitNorm_le_one_smul_eq
declarations.doc:
Rescaling any nonzero element down to the unit ball: `(orderUnitNorm A)⁻¹ • A` has norm at
most `1`, and scaling it back up by `orderUnitNorm A` recovers `A`.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_orderUnitNorm_le_one_smul_eq {A : P.Observables} (hA : orderUnitNorm A ≠ 0) :
    ∃ B : P.Observables, orderUnitNorm B ≤ 1 ∧ orderUnitNorm A • B = A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitAddGroupNorm
declarations.doc: The order-unit norm packaged as an additive-group norm.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def orderUnitAddGroupNorm : AddGroupNorm P.Observables

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNormedAddCommGroup
declarations.doc: The normed additive group given by the order-unit norm.
declarations.statement: noncomputable scoped instance orderUnitNormedAddCommGroup : NormedAddCommGroup P.Observables

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.orderUnitNormedSpace
declarations.doc: The real normed space given by the order-unit norm.
declarations.statement: noncomputable scoped instance orderUnitNormedSpace : NormedSpace ℝ P.Observables

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.isClosed_Ici_zero
declarations.doc: The positive cone is closed in the order-unit-norm topology.
declarations.statement: lemma isClosed_Ici_zero : IsClosed (Set.Ici (0 : P.Observables))

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.closedIciTopology
declarations.doc: Every upper set `[a, ∞)` is closed in the order-unit-norm topology.
declarations.statement: scoped instance closedIciTopology : ClosedIciTopology P.Observables

modules.title: Ordered vector spaces and order units
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

Order-unit spaces capture the basic structure needed for a probabilistic theory: observables,
positivity, effects, states and probabilities. They do this without assuming that the system is
classical or quantum, or that observables have any particular algebraic structure.

In quantum mechanics, the standard example is the real vector space of self-adjoint matrices,
ordered by positive semidefiniteness, with the identity matrix as 1. Keeping only the vector
space, its order, and this distinguished unit gives the abstract order-unit setting.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.exists_two_sided_bound` : every observable sits between `-(n • 1)` and
  `n • 1`, for some `n`.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.exists_real_shift_nonneg` : enough copies of the order unit shift any element
  into the positive cone.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.nonneg_add_eq_zero` : the positive cone meets its negation only at `0`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Ordered vector spaces and order units
- B. Consequences of being an order unit

## iv. References

## B. Consequences of being an order unit

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.one_nonneg
declarations.doc: The certain outcome is nonnegative.
declarations.statement: lemma one_nonneg : 0 ≤ (1 : P.Observables)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.exists_nsmul_one_le
declarations.doc: Every observable is bounded above by a natural multiple of the certain outcome.
declarations.statement: lemma exists_nsmul_one_le (B : P.Observables) : ∃ n : ℕ, B ≤ n • (1 : P.Observables)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.exists_two_sided_bound
declarations.doc: Every element is bounded on both sides by a natural multiple of the order unit.
declarations.statement:
lemma exists_two_sided_bound (A : P.Observables) :
    ∃ n : ℕ, -(n • (1 : P.Observables)) ≤ A ∧ A ≤ n • (1 : P.Observables)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.exists_real_shift_nonneg
declarations.doc:
Every element becomes nonnegative after adding enough copies of the order unit: the positive
cone reaches everywhere, once you're allowed to shift by the unit.
declarations.statement: lemma exists_real_shift_nonneg (A : P.Observables) : ∃ r : ℝ, 0 ≤ r • (1 : P.Observables) + A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.nonneg_add_eq_zero
declarations.doc:
A nonnegative vector that adds with another nonnegative vector to `0` is itself `0`: the
positive cone meets its negation only at `0`.
declarations.statement:
lemma nonneg_add_eq_zero {A B : P.Observables} (hA : 0 ≤ A) (hB : 0 ≤ B) (hAB : A + B = 0) :
    A = 0

modules.title: Ordered positive cones
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

`PosCone P` collects the positive observables of `P`. In quantum mechanics, `P.Observables` is
the real vector space of self-adjoint matrices, whose spectra are real. Its positive cone
consists exactly of those matrices whose spectra are nonnegative.
These elements form a cone: they are closed under addition and scaling by nonnegative reals.

## ii. Key results

- `PosCone` : the cone of positive observables, `PointedCone.positive ℝ P.Observables`. Its
  carrier is exactly `{A | 0 ≤ A}` (`PointedCone.mem_positive`) and it is convex
  (`PointedCone.convex`).
- `PosCone.isClosed` : the positive cone is closed in the order-unit-norm topology of an
  Archimedean order-unit space.
- `PosCone.exists_sub` : every observable is a difference of two positive observables.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The positive cone
- B. Topological closedness
- C. The order unit

declarations.statement: lemma isClosed : IsClosed (PosCone P : Set P.Observables)

lemma coe_nnreal_smul (t : ℝ≥0) (p : PosCone P) :

modules.title: Linear extension from positive observables
modules.doc:
Values on positive observables determine a real-linear functional on all observables.

## i. Overview

Every observable is a difference `p - q` of two positive observables. A map `f` that is additive
and nonnegatively homogeneous on positive observables extends to all observables by sending
`p - q` to `f p - f q`. The value does not depend on the chosen decomposition. The extension is
real-linear and it is the only real-linear map that agrees with `f` on positive observables.

## ii. Key results

- `PosCone.extend` : extend a real-valued map from positive observables.
- `PosCone.extend_sub` : the extension sends every difference `p - q` to `f p - f q`.
- `PosCone.extendₗ` : the extension as a real-linear map.
- `PosCone.extendₗ_unique` : uniqueness among real-linear maps with those values.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The extension
- B. Linearity
- C. Agreement and uniqueness

## iv. References

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.PosCone.extend
declarations.doc:
Extend values on positive observables by `f (p - q) = f p - f q`, for a chosen decomposition
of each observable into positive parts.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def extend (A : P.Observables) : ℝ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.PosCone.extend_sub
declarations.doc: The extension gives `f p - f q` for every decomposition `A = p - q`.
declarations.statement:
lemma extend_sub {A : P.Observables} {p q : PosCone P} (h : (p : P.Observables) - q = A) :
    extend f A = f p - f q

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.PosCone.extend_add
declarations.doc: The extension is additive.
declarations.statement: lemma extend_add (A B : P.Observables) : extend f (A + B) = extend f A + extend f B

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.PosCone.extend_smul
declarations.doc: The extension is homogeneous for every real scalar.
declarations.statement: lemma extend_smul (t : ℝ) (A : P.Observables) : extend f (t • A) = t * extend f A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.PosCone.extendₗ
declarations.doc: The extension as a real-linear map.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def extendₗ : P.Observables →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.PosCone.extendₗ_apply
declarations.doc: The linear extension evaluates as the extension.
declarations.statement: lemma extendₗ_apply (A : P.Observables) : extendₗ f A = extend f A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.PosCone.extend_coe
declarations.doc: The extension agrees with `f` on positive observables.
declarations.statement: lemma extend_coe (p : PosCone P) : extend f (p : P.Observables) = f p

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.PosCone.extendₗ_unique
declarations.doc: Agreement on positive observables determines the real-linear extension.
declarations.statement:
lemma extendₗ_unique (g : P.Observables →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ)
    (h : ∀ p : PosCone P, g (p : P.Observables) = f p) : g = extendₗ f

modules.title: States
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

A state assigns each observable its expectation value. It is a channel into the real numbers:
positive (`0 ≤ A ⟹ 0 ≤ ω A`) and normalized so the certain outcome reads `ω 1 = 1`. In quantum
mechanics, `ω A = tr(ρA)` for a density matrix `ρ`.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.State` : normalized real expectation functionals on observables.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.comap` : pull back a state by evaluating observables through a
  channel.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. States
- B. Transporting states along channels

## iv. References

modules.title: Convex state spaces
modules.doc:
Convexity of the state space and its pure and mixed states.

## i. Overview

States mix: a probabilistic combination of two states is again a state, and the state space
embeds convexly into the algebraic dual. A pure state is one that's never a genuine mixture of
two others, an extreme point of that convex set. A mixed state is one that is a mixture.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.mix` : randomize between two states with a given probability.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.stateSpace_convex` : the state space is convex in the algebraic dual.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.IsPure` : pure states are extreme points of the state space.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.isPure_iff_forall_mix_eq` : a pure state admits only trivial
  genuine mixtures.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.isMixed_iff_exists_mem_openSegment` : mixed states lie between
  two other states.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Mixing states
- B. The state space
- C. Pure and mixed states

## iv. References

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.mix
declarations.doc:
Randomize between two states with probability `t` of choosing the first, so
`t • ω + σ t • φ` with `σ t = 1 - t`.
declarations.statement: abbrev mix (ω φ : P.State) (t : unitInterval) : P.State

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.mix_apply
declarations.doc: Evaluation of a mixture is the pointwise convex combination.
declarations.statement:
lemma mix_apply (ω φ : P.State) (t : unitInterval) (A : P.Observables) :
    mix ω φ t A = (t : ℝ) * ω A + (1 - (t : ℝ)) * φ A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.toLinearMap_mix
declarations.doc: The underlying linear map of a mixture is the corresponding combination of linear maps.
declarations.statement:
lemma toLinearMap_mix (ω φ : P.State) (t : unitInterval) :
    (mix ω φ t).toLinearMap = (t : ℝ) • ω.toLinearMap + (1 - (t : ℝ)) • φ.toLinearMap

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.mix_symm
declarations.doc: Swapping the two states swaps the weights: `σ` is the symmetry of the interval.
declarations.statement: lemma mix_symm (ω φ : P.State) (t : unitInterval) : mix ω φ t = mix φ ω (σ t)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.stateSpace
declarations.doc: States embedded into the algebraic dual.
declarations.statement: abbrev stateSpace : Set (P.Observables →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.stateSpace_convex
declarations.doc: The state space is convex in the algebraic dual.
declarations.statement: lemma stateSpace_convex : Convex ℝ (stateSpace (P := P))

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.IsPure
declarations.doc: A state is pure when it is an extreme point of the state space.
declarations.statement: def IsPure (ω : P.State) : Prop

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.IsMixed
declarations.doc: A state is mixed when it isn't pure.
declarations.statement: def IsMixed (ω : P.State) : Prop

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.isPure_iff_forall_mem_openSegment
declarations.doc: A state is pure exactly when any open segment containing it has both endpoints equal to it.
declarations.statement:
lemma isPure_iff_forall_mem_openSegment {ω : P.State} :
    ω.IsPure ↔ ∀ φ ψ : P.State,
      ω.toLinearMap ∈ openSegment ℝ φ.toLinearMap ψ.toLinearMap → φ = ω ∧ ψ = ω

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.isMixed_iff_exists_mem_openSegment
declarations.doc: A state is mixed exactly when it lies in an open segment with a different endpoint.
declarations.statement:
lemma isMixed_iff_exists_mem_openSegment {ω : P.State} :
    ω.IsMixed ↔ ∃ φ ψ : P.State,
      ω.toLinearMap ∈ openSegment ℝ φ.toLinearMap ψ.toLinearMap ∧ (φ ≠ ω ∨ ψ ≠ ω)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.mem_openSegment_iff_exists_mix
declarations.doc: Open segments between states consist exactly of their genuine mixtures.
declarations.statement:
lemma mem_openSegment_iff_exists_mix (ω φ ψ : P.State) :
    ω.toLinearMap ∈ openSegment ℝ φ.toLinearMap ψ.toLinearMap ↔
      ∃ t : unitInterval, 0 < t ∧ t < 1 ∧ mix φ ψ t = ω

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.isPure_iff_forall_mix_eq
declarations.doc: A state is pure exactly when every genuine binary mixture producing it is trivial.
declarations.statement:
lemma isPure_iff_forall_mix_eq {ω : P.State} :
    ω.IsPure ↔ ∀ φ ψ t, 0 < t → t < 1 → mix φ ψ t = ω → φ = ω ∧ ψ = ω

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.apply_eq_zero_of_mix_eq
declarations.doc:
A positive observable with vanishing expectation in a genuine mixture vanishes in both
components.
declarations.statement:
lemma apply_eq_zero_of_mix_eq {ω φ ψ : P.State} {t : unitInterval} (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1)
    (h : mix φ ψ t = ω) {A : P.Observables} (hA : 0 ≤ A) (hωA : ω A = 0) :
    φ A = 0 ∧ ψ A = 0

modules.title: State discrimination
modules.doc:
Optimal binary discrimination probabilities and their relation to the state distance.

## i. Overview

A system is prepared in state `ω₀` (with probability `p`) or `ω₁` (with probability `1 - p`). We
get to run a single yes/no test on it — an effect `e` — and have to guess which state it was,
based only on whether `e` "clicked". We guess `ω₀` on a click and `ω₁` otherwise; `successProb`
is the probability that guess is right.

Always guessing `ω₁`, without even looking at the system, is already right with probability
`1 - p` — that's our baseline. Running a test can only add to it: its `advantage` is how much
extra success probability it buys over that baseline. Taking the supremum over all tests gives the
classic Helstrom bound (`optimalSuccessProb_eq`), without assuming an optimizing test exists.

For equal priors (`p = 1/2`) the bound simplifies to `1/2 + dist ω₀ ω₁ / 4`.
Two equally likely states are easier to tell apart exactly when they sit farther apart.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.optimalSuccessProb_eq` : the Helstrom bound.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.optimalSuccessProb_half_half_eq` : for equal priors, the bound is the
  state distance.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Success probability and the advantage of a test
- B. The Helstrom bound
- C. Equal priors: the bound is the state distance

## iv. References

- C.W. Helstrom, *Quantum Detection and Estimation Theory*, Academic Press, 1976.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.successProb
declarations.doc:
Probability of guessing right between `ω₀` (prior `p`) and `ω₁` (prior `1 - p`) using test
`e`: guess `ω₀` on a click, `ω₁` otherwise.
declarations.statement: def successProb (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) (p : unitInterval) (e : P.Effect) : ℝ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.advantage
declarations.doc: How much test `e` improves on the baseline of always guessing `ω₁`.
declarations.statement: def advantage (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) (p : unitInterval) (e : P.Effect) : ℝ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.successProb_eq_add_advantage
declarations.doc: Success probability equals the baseline `1 - p` plus the advantage of test `e`.
declarations.statement:
lemma successProb_eq_add_advantage (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) (p : unitInterval) (e : P.Effect) :
    successProb ω₀ ω₁ p e = (1 - p) + advantage ω₀ ω₁ p e

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.advantage_le
declarations.doc: No test's advantage beats the prior weight `p` of the state it favors.
declarations.statement:
lemma advantage_le (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) (p : unitInterval) (e : P.Effect) :
    advantage ω₀ ω₁ p e ≤ p

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.bddAbove_advantage
declarations.doc: Advantages of tests are bounded above.
declarations.statement:
lemma bddAbove_advantage (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) (p : unitInterval) :
    BddAbove (Set.range (advantage ω₀ ω₁ p))

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.optimalSuccessProb
declarations.doc: The best a single test can do.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def optimalSuccessProb (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) (p : unitInterval) : ℝ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.optimalSuccessProb_eq
declarations.doc:
The Helstrom bound: optimal success probability is the baseline `1 - p` plus the best
advantage any test can give.
declarations.statement:
lemma optimalSuccessProb_eq (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) (p : unitInterval) :
    optimalSuccessProb ω₀ ω₁ p = (1 - p) + ⨆ e : P.Effect, advantage ω₀ ω₁ p e

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.sub_complement_eq_neg_sub
declarations.doc: Complementing an effect negates `ω₀ e - ω₁ e`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sub_complement_eq_neg_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) (e : P.Effect) :
    ω₀ (complement e) - ω₁ (complement e) = -(ω₀ e - ω₁ e)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.bddAbove_abs_sub
declarations.doc: The differences `|ω₀ e - ω₁ e|` over effects are bounded above.
declarations.statement:
lemma bddAbove_abs_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) :
    BddAbove (Set.range fun e : P.Effect => |ω₀ e - ω₁ e|)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.bddAbove_sub
declarations.doc: The differences `ω₀ e - ω₁ e` over effects are bounded above.
declarations.statement:
lemma bddAbove_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) :
    BddAbove (Set.range fun e : P.Effect => ω₀ e - ω₁ e)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.ciSup_sub_eq_ciSup_abs_sub
declarations.doc:
The supremum of the state-value difference equals that of its absolute value: complementing
an effect flips the sign.
declarations.statement:
lemma ciSup_sub_eq_ciSup_abs_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) :
    (⨆ e : P.Effect, (ω₀ e - ω₁ e)) = ⨆ e : P.Effect, |ω₀ e - ω₁ e|

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.dist_eq_ciSup_abs_sub
declarations.doc: The state distance is the supremum of the differences on recentered effects.
declarations.statement:
lemma dist_eq_ciSup_abs_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) :
    dist ω₀ ω₁ =
      ⨆ e : P.Effect, |ω₀ (effectEquiv e) - ω₁ (effectEquiv e)|

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.dist_eq_two_mul_ciSup_sub
declarations.doc: The state distance is twice the largest state-value difference over all effects.
declarations.statement:
lemma dist_eq_two_mul_ciSup_sub (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) :
    dist ω₀ ω₁ = 2 * ⨆ e : P.Effect, (ω₀ e - ω₁ e)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.optimalSuccessProb_half_half_eq
declarations.doc: For equal priors, the Helstrom bound is `1/2` plus a quarter of the state distance.
declarations.statement:
lemma optimalSuccessProb_half_half_eq (ω₀ ω₁ : P.State) :
    optimalSuccessProb ω₀ ω₁ ⟨1 / 2, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩ = 1 / 2 + dist ω₀ ω₁ / 4

modules.title: States of a local net
modules.doc:
Compatible subsystem states and states of the whole system.

## i. Overview

An observable of a smaller subsystem can also be measured in a larger one. A state of the larger
subsystem therefore determines a state of the smaller one: assign each smaller observable the
expectation it has when viewed in the larger system. This operation is called restriction.
Observable inclusions point from smaller to larger subsystems, state restrictions point the other
way.

In a tensor product system, including an observable means letting it act as the identity on the
additional factors. Restricting a density-matrix state then amounts to tracing out those factors.
A `LocalNet.CompatibleStates` assigns a state to every subsystem, with the requirement that a
smaller subsystem's state agrees with the restriction of any larger subsystem's state. Thus the
expectation of an observable does not depend on which containing subsystem is used to evaluate
it.

For a nonempty directed family, local positivity defines an order on the quasilocal observables.
Every compatible family then defines a unique state of the whole system. Conversely, a quasilocal
state restricts to a compatible family of subsystem states.

## ii. Key results

- `LocalNet.restrict`: precomposition with the observable inclusion map.
- `LocalNet.CompatibleStates`: a compatible family of states on the subsystems.
- `LocalNet.CompatibleStates.compat_apply`: compatible states agree on included observables.
- `LocalNet.toState`: the quasilocal state defined by a compatible family.
- `LocalNet.stateEquiv`: quasilocal states correspond to compatible local states.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Restriction of states
- B. Compatible local states
- C. States of the whole system

## iv. References

sections.text:
## B. Compatible local states

A compatible family assigns a state to every local subsystem. Whenever one subsystem is contained
in another, its state must agree with the restriction of the larger subsystem's state. This
ensures that local observables have consistent expectation values, even in infinite systems with
correlations and entanglement.

## C. States of the whole system

A quasilocal observable has a local representative. A compatible family evaluates that
representative in its subsystem; compatibility makes the result independent of the representative.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.restrict
declarations.doc: Restrict a state of `Y` to `X` by pulling it back along the observable inclusion channel.
declarations.statement: def restrict (N : LocalNet R A) (h : X ≤ Y) (ω : (A Y).State) : (A X).State

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.restrict_apply
declarations.doc: Restriction evaluates an observable through its inclusion into the larger subsystem.
declarations.statement:
lemma restrict_apply (N : LocalNet R A) (h : X ≤ Y) (ω : (A Y).State) (a : (A X).Observables) :
    N.restrict h ω a = ω (N.incl h a)

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.restrict_refl
declarations.doc: Restriction to the same subsystem is the identity.
declarations.statement: lemma restrict_refl (N : LocalNet R A) (ω : (A X).State) : N.restrict (le_refl X) ω = ω

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.restrict_restrict
declarations.doc: Successive restrictions agree with direct restriction.
declarations.statement:
lemma restrict_restrict (N : LocalNet R A) (h₁ : X ≤ Y) (h₂ : Y ≤ Z) (h₃ : X ≤ Z)
    (ω : (A Z).State) :
    N.restrict h₁ (N.restrict h₂ ω) = N.restrict h₃ ω

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.CompatibleStates
declarations.doc: A state on each subsystem whose restrictions agree with the states of smaller subsystems.
declarations.statement:
structure CompatibleStates (N : LocalNet R A) where
  /-- The state of the subsystem `X`. -/
  state : ∀ X, (A X).State
  /-- The state of `X` is the restriction of the state of any larger subsystem `Y`. -/
  compat : ∀ {X Y : R} (h : X ≤ Y), N.restrict h (state Y) = state X

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.CompatibleStates.compat_apply
declarations.doc: An observable has the same expectation in every subsystem containing it.
declarations.statement:
lemma CompatibleStates.compat_apply {N : LocalNet R A} (ω : N.CompatibleStates)
    {X Y : R} (h : X ≤ Y) (a : (A X).Observables) :
    ω.state Y (N.incl h a) = ω.state X a

declarations.doc: Decidable equality used internally by the direct-limit construction.
declarations.statement: noncomputable local instance : DecidableEq R

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.lift
declarations.doc: The expectation functional of `LocalNet.CompatibleStates` on the whole system.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def lift (σ : N.CompatibleStates) : N.Quasilocal →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.lift_apply
declarations.doc:
The expectation functional of `LocalNet.CompatibleStates` evaluates a quasilocal observable
in any subsystem representing it.
declarations.statement:
lemma lift_apply (σ : N.CompatibleStates) (i : R) (a : (A i).Observables) :
    lift σ (toQuasilocal N i a) = σ.state i a

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toState
declarations.doc: The state of the whole system defined by `LocalNet.CompatibleStates`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def toState (σ : N.CompatibleStates) : N.quasilocalTheory.State

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.toState_apply
declarations.doc: On a quasilocal observable represented in the subsystem `i`, `toState σ` is the state of `i`.
declarations.statement:
lemma toState_apply (σ : N.CompatibleStates) (i : R) (a : (A i).Observables) :
    toState σ (toQuasilocal N i a) = σ.state i a

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.LocalNet.stateEquiv
declarations.doc: A state of the whole system is the same as `LocalNet.CompatibleStates`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def stateEquiv : N.quasilocalTheory.State ≃ N.CompatibleStates

modules.title: The metric space of states
modules.doc:
The operator-norm distance between states and their distance to the set of pure states.

## i. Overview

A state is just a positive linear functional — no continuity is assumed. It turns out to be
automatically bounded: `|ω A| ≤ ‖A‖`. Physically, a state can never predict
an expectation value bigger than what the observable itself can read.

That bound induces a genuine operator-norm distance between states, `dist`, making `P.State` a
`MetricSpace`. It also defines `distToPure`, the infimum distance to the set of pure states.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.abs_apply_le_orderUnitNorm` : a state's values are bounded by the
  order-unit norm.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.dist` : the operator-norm distance between states.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.distToPure` : a state's infimum distance to the set of pure states.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. States are bounded by the order-unit norm
- B. The state metric
- C. Distance to pure states

## iv. References

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.apply_le_one
declarations.doc: A state takes values at most `1` on observables bounded by the unit.
declarations.statement: lemma apply_le_one (ω : P.State) {A : P.Observables} (hA : A ≤ 1) : ω A ≤ 1

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.apply_le_orderUnitNorm
declarations.doc: A state never overshoots the order-unit norm.
declarations.statement: lemma apply_le_orderUnitNorm (ω : P.State) (A : P.Observables) : ω A ≤ orderUnitNorm A

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.abs_apply_le_orderUnitNorm

declarations.statement: lemma abs_apply_le_orderUnitNorm (ω : P.State) (A : P.Observables) : |ω A| ≤ orderUnitNorm A

Two states' predictions on any observable of order-unit norm at most `1` never differ by more
than `2`.

    |ω A - φ A| ≤ 2

The values `|ω A - φ A|` of two states, restricted to the order-unit-norm unit ball, are
bounded by `2`.

lemma dist_bddAbove (ω φ : P.State) :
    BddAbove (Set.range fun A : {A : P.Observables // orderUnitNorm A ≤ 1} => |ω A - φ A|)

declarations.doc:
The operator-norm distance between two states: how far apart their predictions can get on an
observable of order-unit norm at most `1`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def dist (ω φ : P.State) : ℝ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.dist_nonneg
declarations.doc: Distances between states are nonnegative.
declarations.statement: lemma dist_nonneg (ω φ : P.State) : 0 ≤ dist ω φ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.dist_le_two
declarations.doc: The whole state space has diameter at most `2`: it's a bounded metric space.
declarations.statement: lemma dist_le_two (ω φ : P.State) : dist ω φ ≤ 2

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.dist_self
declarations.statement: lemma dist_self (ω : P.State) : dist ω ω = 0

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.dist_comm
declarations.doc: The state distance is symmetric.
declarations.statement: lemma dist_comm (ω φ : P.State) : dist ω φ = dist φ ω

declarations.doc: The state distance satisfies the triangle inequality.

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.eq_of_dist_eq_zero
declarations.doc: `dist` separates states: two states at distance `0` are equal.
declarations.statement: lemma eq_of_dist_eq_zero {ω φ : P.State} (h : dist ω φ = 0) : ω = φ

A state's value at a doubled, re-centered effect (`effectEquiv`) is twice its value at
the effect, minus one.

lemma apply_effectEquiv (ψ : P.State) (e : P.Effect) :
    ψ (effectEquiv e) = 2 * ψ e - 1

declarations.statement: noncomputable instance instMetricSpace : MetricSpace P.State

declarations.statement: noncomputable def distToPure (ω : P.State) : ℝ

declarations.doc: The distance to the set of pure states is nonnegative.
declarations.statement: lemma distToPure_nonneg (ω : P.State) : 0 ≤ distToPure ω

declarations.statement: lemma distToPure_eq_zero_of_isPure {ω : P.State} (h : IsPure ω) : distToPure ω = 0

modules.title: The state–effect pairing
modules.doc:
State–effect evaluation gives probabilities that distinguish states and effects alike.

## i. Overview

Evaluating an effect in a state gives a probability, and evaluation is affine in the effect.
A state is determined by its probabilities on all effects. Conversely, an effect is determined
by its probabilities in all states. The pairing therefore separates both sides.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.apply_mem_Icc` : state–effect evaluation takes values in `[0, 1]`.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.apply_mix` : evaluation is affine in the effect argument.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.ext_of_effect_eq` : effects separate states.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.ext_of_forall_apply_eq` : states separate effects.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. State–effect evaluation
- B. Effects separate states
- C. States separate effects

## iv. References

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.apply_mem_Icc
declarations.doc: State–effect evaluation takes values in `[0, 1]`.
declarations.statement: lemma apply_mem_Icc (ω : P.State) (e : P.Effect) : ω e ∈ Set.Icc 0 1

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.apply_mix
declarations.doc: Evaluation is affine in the effect argument.
declarations.statement:
lemma apply_mix (ω : P.State) (e f : P.Effect) (t : unitInterval) :
    ω (Effect.mix e f t) = (t : ℝ) * ω e + (1 - (t : ℝ)) * ω f

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.State.ext_of_effect_eq
declarations.doc: A state is determined by its values on effects.
declarations.statement: lemma ext_of_effect_eq {ω φ : P.State} (h : ∀ e : P.Effect, ω e = φ e) : ω = φ

declarations.name: ProbabilisticTheory.Effect.ext_of_forall_apply_eq

declarations.statement:
lemma ext_of_forall_apply_eq {e f : P.Effect}
    (h : ∀ ω : P.State, ω e = ω f) : e = f

modules.title: Separation by states
modules.doc:
States determine positivity, the order-unit norm, and equality of observables.

## i. Overview

In an Archimedean order-unit space, states determine the entire ordered normed structure. An
element is positive exactly when every state assigns it a nonnegative value, and its order-unit
norm is `‖A‖₁ = sup { |ω A| : ω a state }`. Consequently, states separate points: two elements are
equal whenever every state assigns them the same value.

The main ingredient is Hahn–Banach separation of a point from the positive cone. Applied to an
element `A ≱ 0`, it produces a state `ω` with `ω A < 0`. Everything else follows from this one
separation fact.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.exists_apply_neg_of_not_nonneg` : every element outside the positive
  cone is separated from it by a state.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.nonneg_iff_forall_state_nonneg` : states determine the positive cone.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.sSup_abs_apply_eq_orderUnitNorm` : states determine the order-unit
  norm.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.ext_of_forall_apply_eq` : states separate points.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Separating points from the cone
- B. The positive cone
- C. The order-unit norm
- D. Separation of points

## iv. References

declarations.doc: A positive functional vanishing at the order unit vanishes everywhere.
declarations.statement:
lemma apply_eq_zero_of_apply_one_eq_zero {p : P.Observables →ₚ[ℝ] ℝ}

    ∃ ω : P.State, ω A < 0

declarations.doc: An element is positive iff every state assigns it a nonnegative value.
declarations.statement: lemma nonneg_iff_forall_state_nonneg (A : P.Observables) : 0 ≤ A ↔ ∀ ω : P.State, 0 ≤ ω A

    orderUnitNorm A ≤ r ↔ ∀ ω : P.State, |ω A| ≤ r

Reversible changes of observables act on states by inverse pullback.

## i. Overview

A state is invariant under a group action when every transformation leaves it fixed.
Pullback along an intertwining channel preserves this invariance.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.IsInvariant` : states fixed by a group action.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.IsInvariant.comap` : pullback preserves invariant states.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Reversible action
- B. Invariant states

## iv. References

modules.title: States as weights
modules.doc:
Restriction of a state to positive observables gives a finite normalized weight.

## i. Overview

State values are nonnegative on the positive cone. Reading them as extended nonnegative
reals produces a weight with value one on the certain outcome.

## ii. Key results

- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.toWeight` : the weight induced by a state.
- `ProbabilisticTheory.State.toWeight_isState` : finiteness and normalization.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. From a state to a weight

## iv. References

declarations.doc:
The weight induced by a state: `ENNReal.ofReal` applied to the state's values on the positive
cone, where they are automatically nonnegative.

lemma toWeight_apply (s : P.State) (A : PosCone P) :
    s.toWeight A = ENNReal.ofReal (s (A : P.Observables))

declarations.doc: The weight induced by a state agrees with the state itself on the positive cone.

    (s.toWeight A).toReal = s (A : P.Observables)

declarations.statement: lemma toWeight_isState (s : P.State) : s.toWeight.IsState

modules.title: Weights
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

A state assigns each positive observable a nonnegative expectation value, normalized so the
certain outcome reads exactly `1`. A *weight* generalizes this by dropping the normalization and
letting the values be extended nonnegative reals, possibly `+∞`. This matters especially in
infinite dimensions: the trace on `B(H)` is only finite on the trace-class operators and genuinely
diverges to `+∞` elsewhere. A state is then the special case that happens to be finite everywhere
and normalized.

## ii. Key results

- `Weight.monotone` : weights are monotone on the positive cone.
- `Weight.IsFinite.isSemifinite` : a finite weight is automatically semifinite.
- `Weight.IsFinite.normalize_isState` : rescaling a finite weight that's nonzero at the order unit
  turns it into a state.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Weights
- B. States as weights

## iv. References

- G. Ludwig, *Foundations of Quantum Mechanics I*, Springer, 1983.
  <https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-86751-4>

declarations.doc: A finite weight is semifinite.

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.toReal_map_add
declarations.doc: A finite weight's real value is additive.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsFinite.toReal_map_add {w : Weight P} (hw : w.IsFinite) (A B : PosCone P) :
    (w (A + B)).toReal = (w A).toReal + (w B).toReal

declarations.name: Weight.toReal_map_nnreal_smul
declarations.doc: A weight's real value scales linearly under nonnegative real scaling.
declarations.statement:
lemma toReal_map_nnreal_smul (w : Weight P) (k : ℝ≥0) (A : PosCone P) :
    (w (k • A)).toReal = k * (w A).toReal

declarations.name: Weight.IsNormal
declarations.doc:
A weight is normal when it preserves least upper bounds of increasing sequences in the
positive cone.

declarations.name: Weight.IsState
declarations.doc: A weight that's finite everywhere and gives the certain outcome weight exactly `1`.
declarations.statement:
structure IsState (w : Weight P) : Prop where
  /-- A state is finite everywhere. -/
  finite : w.IsFinite
  /-- A state gives the certain outcome weight exactly `1`. -/
  normalized : w 1 = 1

declarations.name: Weight.normalize
declarations.doc: Rescale a weight by the inverse of its value at the order unit.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def normalize (w : Weight P) : Weight P

declarations.name: Weight.normalize_apply
declarations.statement:
lemma normalize_apply (w : Weight P) (A : PosCone P) :
    normalize w A = (w 1)⁻¹ * w A

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.normalize_isFinite
declarations.doc: Normalizing a finite weight that's nonzero at the order unit keeps it finite.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsFinite.normalize_isFinite {w : Weight P} (hw : w.IsFinite) (h : w 1 ≠ 0) :
    (normalize w).IsFinite

declarations.name: Weight.IsFinite.normalize_isState
declarations.doc:
Normalizing a finite weight that's nonzero at the order unit makes it a state: the order unit
is scaled to weight exactly `1`.
declarations.statement:
lemma IsFinite.normalize_isState {w : Weight P} (hw : w.IsFinite) (h : w 1 ≠ 0) :
    (normalize w).IsState

modules.doc:
Finite normalized weights correspond exactly to states.

## i. Overview

A finite normalized weight extends linearly to a state. Restriction to positive observables
recovers the original weight, giving an equivalence.

## ii. Key results

- `Weight.IsState.toState` : extend a finite normalized weight to a state.
- `Weight.stateEquiv` : the correspondence with states.
